rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The play at a glance "Refund" by Fritz Karinthy is a Hungarian one-act satire with a simple, gleeful premise: a man returns to his old school eighteen years after graduating — without learning anything, he claims — and demands his tuition fees back.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Satire on education: Wasserkopf demands his tuition back because he learned nothing.
The teachers 'win' by out-examining him — clever twist saves the money.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: The mathematics master's final move (any answer can be 'wrong' or 'right') shows education's real lesson: thinking, not facts — quote the last exchange.  ·  ## The characters worth an essay **Wasserkopf** is the comic engine: boastful, litigious, quick-tongued and genuinely defeated by a single honest number. The sketch the exam wants holds his contradiction — he is the class failure, yet his quibbling eloquence is school-taught; his ignorance is real, but his argument is educated. His defeat is satisfying because it is earned by his own demand.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## The themes worth an essay **The worth of education** — the central theme: what does schooling actually give? The play's answer is double — the pupil learned less than the school hoped and more than he admits; the compound-interest calculation is the proof on both sides.…  ·  ## NEB short answers, solved **Q. Why does Wasserkopf return to his school? (2 marks)** A. To demand a refund of his tuition fees, with compound interest, on the ground that his education failed him: eighteen years after graduating he is unfit for life, and he holds the school responsible. He backs the demand with the threat of a newspaper scandal. **Q. How do the masters react to his demand? (2 marks)** A.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. Why does Wasserkopf demand a refund? (2 marks) — he claims eighteen years of schooling taught him nothing useful; he wants his fees back with interest.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ## NEB long answers, solved **Q. "Refund is a satire on both the school and the pupil." Discuss. (8 marks)** A model answer satirises both sides with evidence: the school's panic over scandal, its masters' confidence and their serial defeat by their own disciplines, and the pupil's genuine ignorance wrapped in genuinely educated argument.…

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The action, scene by scene The play opens with the threat: Wasserkopf — the name means "water-head", and the masters remember him fondly as the class's most distinguished failure — arrives demanding his tuition refunded, with compound interest, because the education he received has left him unfit for life.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Satire** — the play's genre and its point: education examined by its worst product, and the examination exposing both the school's anxiety about reputation and the pupil's confidence in his own ignorance.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Satire target: the education system that certifies without wisdom — Wasserkopf's absurd demand for a refund exposes what schooling failed to teach.  ·  Trick 2: The teachers' counter-trick: they declare him a GENIUS, using his own logic against him — the reversal is the play's climax; explain the logic trap.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. How do the teachers defeat him? (2 marks) — by proving every answer he gives is correct (each wrong answer 'proves' his genius), so no refund is due.
